profile.behavior: Highly active insectivore that flits through foliage, gleans prey, and darts after insects in flight. Frequently flicks and fans its wings and tail to flush prey; migrates mostly at night and defends territories.
field_marks: Small, slim warbler with a broad, flat black bill and dark eye
Adult male mostly black with vivid orange patches on the sides, wings, and tail
Female and immature male gray and olive-brown with yellow to yellow-orange patches
Pale white to gray belly contrasts with the darker upperparts
Fairly long dark tail with colored basal panels; legs and feet black
profile.habitat: Moist, open deciduous and mixed woodland, especially second-growth forest with a dense shrubby layer; also thickets and streamside woods. During migration it uses varied wooded or shrubby habitats, while nonbreeding habitats include forest, scrub, and mangroves.

findings: Live sources confirm the identity as American Redstart, Setophaga ruticilla, family Parulidae.

The printed length 11–13 cm (4.3–5.1 in), weight 6–9 g (0.2–0.3 oz), and wingspan 16–19 cm (6.3–7.5 in) exactly match Cornell's published ranges. Audubon publishes a slightly broader 16–20 cm wingspan, but this does not invalidate the directly supported Cornell range.
Every visible prose line, name, measurement, and field-mark statement matches the proposed text without spelling, number, word-order, duplication, omission, or substitution errors.

The primary specimen is identifiable as an adult male: black head and upperparts, white lower underparts, vivid orange side patches, orange wing patches, and orange basal tail panels agree with the male reference photos and live descriptions.

The bill is short, dark, pointed, and relatively broad and flat; both primary and supplementary heads have coherent, consistently proportioned, co-terminal mandibles. The eye, legs, feet, folded wing, and long tail are structurally plausible. The primary bird is slightly fuller-bodied than the clearest references but remains within plausible posture variation.

The primary specimen is a single lateral-view bird with one head, one beak, two legs, two anatomically implied wings (the far wing is naturally occluded), and one tail. No attached duplicate anatomy is present.

The detached wing and head are clearly separate supplementary studies. Both are coherent and do not appear attached to the primary specimen; the wing correctly emphasizes the orange basal flight-feather region.

The body-length ruler repeats the verified 11–13 cm (4.3–5.1 in) range, has matching units, two endpoints, and exactly four evenly spaced unlabeled interior ticks forming five proportional segments. No conflicting marker appears, and “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE” clearly prevents interpretation as the printed bird's physical size.
The five swatches correspond in order to coal black, flame orange, golden yellow, soft gray, and creamy white, consistent with the plate text and documented plumages.
No place name, ZIP code, coordinates, map, or local-observation detail appears.
